Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Proposition 1
Should the state be authorized to issue $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to support building and preserving affordable housing, expanding homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income residents, veterans and homelessness programs?
The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 would authorize a general obligation bond, $10 billion of which would fund affordable housing and related infrastructure projects. Another $1.25 billion would fund the CalVet Home Loan Program. The Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026) reports bond funds would support up to 40,000 rental units and could also assist 40,000 families in buying a home.
Yes Argument
Proposition 1 builds and preserves affordable homes and expands homeownership opportunities without raising taxes. It unlocks federal matching funds and fast-tracks construction. This measure will benefit veterans, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, at-risk foster youth, working families and people with disabilities.
No Argument
This package represents $11 billion in debt that taxpayers will add to their credit card with no reforms. We know the cost of building in California is exponentially higher than it needs to be. We have to reform that by first cutting costly regulations before we take out the credit card and borrow money.

Proposition 1
Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
California needs more money for housing in order to help the state’s more than 180,000 homeless residents, as well as those who pay more than they can afford in rent and those who can’t afford to purchase a home.
Oppose
Some Republican legislators criticized the bill for using veterans to drum up support while actually doing little to serve them. They also questioned the wisdom of borrowing more money to pay for housing without addressing the underlying reasons it’s so expensive to build.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.

HJTA’S QUICK VOTING GUIDE
YES on
39, 41, 42, 43, 45
NO
on
1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 37, 38, 40, 44
NO on Prop. 1
Called the “Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” this is $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds with only $1.25 billion allocated to benefit veterans. The rest will finance other housing assistance programs. Bonds are borrowed money. Like all general obligation bonds, the actual cost to taxpayers will be roughly double the advertised amount due to interest that must be paid to investors. Bonds are the most expensive way to pay for anything, and when used to pay for programs instead of capital projects, it’s a much greater burden on taxpayers than just paying for these programs from the budget.
Vote NO on 1 .
NO on Prop. 2
This measure makes changes to the Gann Limit, passed by voters in 1979, and to the rules for the Budget Stabilization Account (“Rainy Day Fund”) that were approved by voters in 2014. Tax revenue goes up and down in California with the stock market, because of the state’s dependence on taxes from high earners and capital gains. Proposition 2 attempts to address this revenue volatility challenge with new rules for the Budget Stabilization Account. However, while Prop. 2 addresses the treatment of appropriations into and out of reserve funds in a way that makes sense from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility, it doesn’t address the weakening of the Gann Limit by Propositions 98 (1988) and 111 (1990), enabling reckless overspending that has led to structural deficits and self-inflicted budget “emergencies.” California is in desperate need of fiscal discipline. The changes in the state constitution that permit unlimited spending should be reversed. Prop. 2 falls far short of real spending reform and, unfortunately, amounts to little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb.
Vote NO on 2 .
NO on Prop. 3
Remember the “temporary” income tax rate hike “for the schools” that was passed in 2012 and “temporarily” renewed in 2016? This measure renews it again and this time makes it permanent. California has the highest income tax rates in the nation, and every year the state has a bigger budget and a higher cost of living to show for it. These “temporary” income tax rate hikes should not be a backdoor method for permanent tax increases.
Vote NO on 3 .
NO on Prop. 4
Existing law, the Political Reform Act of 1974 (PRA), prohibits the use of tax money to finance political campaigns for elective office. Proposition 4 would remove that ban. HJTA has previously won court cases upholding this provision of the PRA, and we haven’t changed our position. Taxpayers should not have to pay the campaign expenses of candidates running for office or incumbents running for re-election.
Vote NO on 4 .
NO on Prop. 5
This measure alters the constitutional right to recall a state officer and vote for a replacement candidate. Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate in recalls of statewide officeholders and state legislators. Offices would be filled by appointment or later special election. If a governor was recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor for the remainder of the unexpired term or until a special election, depending on timing. Proposition 5 allows the recalled officeholder to run in the special election to fill the seat, which current law prohibits. This measure makes a mockery of the recall process.
Vote NO on 5 .
NO on Prop. 37
This measure authorizes $25 billion in bonds for a program that would offer second-mortgage loans for down payments on newly constructed or converted homes (not existing homes) to eligible buyers who earn less than 200% of the area median income. Although there is no direct cost to taxpayers, a market downturn could cause mass foreclosures if stretched borrowers are unable to make their payments or sell the home for what they owe. Investors bear the financial risks, but the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) must manage this massive pool of funds to protect the bondholders and pay them the interest they are owed. HJTA appreciates the intent of this measure, but we have concerns about the size of the program and the criteria for eligibility to participate. Prop. 37 is not a constitutional amendment, which leaves it subject to legislative alteration. More fundamentally, California’s housing crisis is better addressed with less government impediments to building rather than a new government program. We urge a No vote.
Vote NO on 37 .
NO on Prop. 38
Another bond measure, Proposition 38 authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for research and therapies related to using the body’s immune system to treat disease. There is no reason that this cost should be borne by California taxpayers. Viable research can be funded by pharmaceutical companies, foundations and the federal government. An analysis by CalMatters reveals that the ballot language criteria were tailored in a way that very likely excludes all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. Prop. 38 appears to be a clear case of self-dealing at the expense of taxpayers.
Vote NO on 38 .
YES on Prop. 39
Proposition 39 is the Voter ID initiative. While 36 states currently require some form of voter ID, California isn’t one of them. Voter ID is used successfully around the country to prevent voter impersonation at the polls and to ensure that mail ballots are validly submitted by eligible voters. It’s especially important to California taxpayers to secure our elections from the potential for fraud, because billions of dollars of tax measures are on the ballot in nearly every election.
Vote YES on 39 .
NO on Prop. 40
This is the “wealth tax,” supposedly affecting only billionaires but in fact a threat to every California taxpayer and homeowner. Proposition 40 imposes a “one-time tax” of 5% of “covered assets” valued above $1 billion. However, the measure includes language that allows the Legislature to rewrite the law later, potentially changing the thresholds, the assets that are covered, the percentage to be taken, and the number of times the tax would be levied. This is an entirely new type of tax, and we don’t know where it will lead. Will all Californians have to submit forms to the Franchise Tax Board declaring their assets every year? How much will ordinary Californians have to pay for “wealth tax preparation” to comply with this law?
Vote NO on 40 .
YES on Prop. 41
This measure requires pre-election audits of programs that would be funded by new statewide special taxes. It’s a good idea to find out where the existing funds are going before voters are asked to approve higher taxes for the same programs.
Vote YES on 41 .
YES on Prop. 42
In direct opposition to the “wealth tax,” this measure would prohibit any new state tax that taxes the ownership or control of personal property or applies retroactively based on activities or status that existed before the effective date of the new state tax. This will protect Californians, especially homeowners, from the risk of a “wealth tax” on the value of homes or any other accumulated savings and investments.
Vote YES on 42 .
YES on Prop. 43
Proposition 43 is the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 . It restores Prop. 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Prop. 43 closes the court-created “Upland” loophole that has allowed special interest groups to write their own tax increases, direct the money to themselves, collect signatures to place them on the ballot and then evade the two-thirds vote requirement. Because of this loophole, Californians are paying billions of dollars in taxes that they should not have had to pay.
Vote YES on 43 and tell a friend!
NO on Prop. 44
This measure requires community clinics that provide primary care to medically underserved areas and populations to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient services, not management and overhead. It authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance on qualifying expenditures and lets the Department of Public Health issue waivers. It authorizes monetary penalties and criminal charges. It is sponsored by a powerful labor organization seeking to expand its control over private clinics.
Vote NO on 44 .
YES on Prop. 45
Few things have impeded rational housing policy in the state more than the California Environmental Quality Act. It slows down development which, in turn, limits housing supply, increasing the cost of living. Far from being a tool to address legitimate environment concerns, it has been used more frequently as leverage by labor organizations to exact favorable labor agreements. While CEQA reform to prevent excessive delays is necessary, Proposition 45 is not perfect since it carves out only certain projects for reform and locks in costly labor agreements. It also creates opportunities for government to pick winners and losers. But while HJTA would prefer a full revamp of CEQA, Prop. 45 is a good first step.
Vote YES on 45 .
LOCAL BALLOT MEASURE RECOMMENDATIONS
City of Los Angeles
NO on Measure FD
This is a one-half percent sales tax increase in the city of L.A. with the revenue earmarked for the fire department. We oppose this measure because the sales tax in Los Angeles will already rise to 10.25% in October because of Measure ER passing in L.A. County in June, and because the City Council and the Mayor should fully fund the fire department from the existing budget of approximately $15 billion without a tax increase. This measure is a special tax that should require a two-thirds vote to pass, but courts have allowed “citizens’ initiative tax increases,” placed on the ballot by collecting signatures, to pass with fewer votes. HJTA’s ballot measure, the Local Taxpayer Protection Act to Save Proposition 13 (Proposition 43 on the November ballot) will close the loophole, but this tax increase, if approved by just 50% plus one vote, will squeeze through it before Proposition 43 takes effect in January.
City of Santa Monica
NO on Measure ES
This is a parcel tax, an extra $495 per taxable parcel of property every year, adjusted annually for inflation. The revenue is earmarked for schools. Special taxes are required by the constitution to be approved by two-thirds of voters, but this is another “citizens’ initiative tax increase” rushing to squeeze through the court-created “Upland” loophole before voters approve Proposition 43 in November.
City of Palos Verdes Estates
NO on Measure PVE
This is a renewal of a parcel tax with a massive increase in the per-parcel rate from $342 to $1,025 to pay for police services and “to pay down the City's unfunded accrued pension liability.” City voters previously rejected a different measure in June to renew and increase the temporary parcel tax.
El Dorado County
NO on Measure S
Measure S is a 30-year countywide sales tax increase. It would raise the sales tax by 3/8 percent. Marshall Medical Center is sponsoring the campaign for the tax. The Yes on S website states that “Marshall receives revenue to support $125M in bond issuance to fund capital improvements.” El Dorado County has only two hospitals: Marshall Medical Center and Barton Memorial Hospital. Measure S is structured so Marshall qualifies for the hospital funding while Barton does not. South Lake Tahoe residents would still pay the countywide tax even though Barton falls below the measure’s hospital eligibility threshold.
Five-County Bay Area
NO on regional transit sales tax
This is a sales tax increase of at least one-half percent (1% in San Francisco) in five Bay Area counties (San Francisco, Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara) to fund transit. Critics rightly argue that the longstanding financial and management problems of transit systems in the Bay Area will not be fixed with another tax increase. Beyond that, a higher sales tax burdens people who already pay high sales taxes and are struggling with the high cost of living. This measure, too, is a “citizens’ initiative tax increase” attempting to get through the court-created loophole before HJTA closes it with Proposition 43.

Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.

California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.

The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:
The largest line, $5.1 billion, goes to the Department of Housing and Community Development's Multifamily Housing Program, which lends to developers of new and renovated apartments in exchange for rent limits. The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. There’s a $11.25 billion housing bond on the ballot this November. Here’s what you should know

By Marisa Kendall, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 aims to address that crisis.

It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. 

A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes.

Legislators have passed multiple laws trying to address that by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. 

A recent report estimated nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.

Californians Head to Polls in Historically Sour Mood; Billionaire Wealth Tax Slips below Majority Support
BECERRA PRESERVES WIDE LEAD OVER HILTON; ENTHUSIASM GAP FAVORS DEMOCRATS IN CONGRESSIONAL RACES; SOLID MAJORITY FAVOR HIGH-EARNER INCOME TAX MEASURE

SAN FRANCISCO, October 27, 2026—A week ahead of Election Day, Californians are exceptionally pessimistic about the direction of the country, the state, and the economy. Support for a high-profile initiative that would tax billionaires appears to be eroding. Democrat Xavier Becerra maintains a commanding lead over Republican Steve Hilton in the race for governor. And Democrats are far more excited than Republicans or independents about voting in congressional races. These are among the key findings from a statewide survey released today by the Public Policy Institute of California.
Eighty-two percent of adult Californians think things in the United States are generally going in the wrong direction, the highest share holding this pessimistic view since PPIC began asking about the national outlook two decades ago. Nearly eight in ten predict bad economic conditions in both the state and the nation over the next 12 months, a high not matched since the depths of the pandemic and Great Recession.
“If you’re looking for one word to describe Californians’ mood as they are filling out their ballots, it would be gloomy—very gloomy,” said Mark Baldassare, PPIC Statewide Survey director and Miller Chair in Public Policy. “Affordability continues to be a central concern, with majorities across demographic groups saying their incomes are not keeping up with inflation.”
In the race for governor, Democrat Xavier Becerra has a 24 point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (61% to 37%), including a 13 point lead among independent likely voters. Californians say they are largely satisfied with their choices for governor, although that satisfaction appears to vary significantly by age: while nearly 70 percent of likely voters 55 and older are pleased with their gubernatorial choices, only half of younger voters aged 18 to 34 are satisfied.
More key findings from the survey:
Billionaire wealth tax falls below majority support: Forty-six percent of likely voters say they will vote yes on Proposition 40, a controversial citizens’ initiative that would impose a one-time tax of up to 5 percent on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion. Last month, 52 percent of likely voters said they would support the measure.
“Since last month, we’ve seen declining support for Prop 40, particularly among Democrats and independents,” said Baldassare. “Propositions 41 and 42, which could effectively nullify Prop 40 even if it was passed, are now polling better than the billionaire tax.”
While support for the billionaire wealth tax appears to be eroding, a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would make a temporary marginal income tax on high earners permanent. Among Democrats, 80 percent support Proposition 3, while 64 percent support the billionaire wealth tax.
Enthusiasm gap favors Democrats in congressional races: Seventy-one percent of Democratic likely voters say they are more enthusiastic than usual about voting in congressional elections, compared to 46 percent of Republicans. The partisan enthusiasm gap is larger than it was ahead of the 2024 general election.
Unhappiness with the Trump administration is likely playing a role. Seventy-eight percent of California adults disapprove of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president—the president’s highest disapproval rating among Californians during his two terms in office. Since the beginning of the year, the president’s approval ratings have dropped most acutely among independents, from 25 percent in February to 16 percent in October.
Majorities back bond measures, oppose tax restrictions: Majorities of California likely voters back the three borrowing measures on the November ballot. More than 60 percent support Propositions 1 and 37, which would authorize tens of billions in bonds for housing programs. Fifty-seven percent say they will vote yes on Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds for immunology research. A majority also support Proposition 2, which increases the amount of revenue the state can deposit into a rainy day fund.
A majority of likely voters oppose Proposition 43, which would make it more difficult to increase local taxes. A slim majority oppose Proposition 45 (50% oppose, 46% approve), which would modify the state’s marquee environmental law to speed construction of some new developments.
Californians are skeptical about the need for voter ID: Nearly 60 percent of likely voters oppose Proposition 39, a citizens’ initiative that would require government-issued ID at the polls. Despite federal allegations of rampant voter fraud, 63 percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
About the Survey
The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The findings are based on responses from 1,728 California adult residents. The sampling error is ±3.0 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample and ±3.8 percent for the 1,086 likely voters. Interviewing took place from October 16–22, 2026. For more information, please see the methodology section in the full survey report.
Mark Baldassare is statewide survey director at PPIC, where he holds the Arjay and Frances Fearing Miller Chair in Public Policy. He is founder of the PPIC Statewide Survey, which he has directed since 1998.
